name: Delay and reverb
seoDesc: Delay and reverb: work out note length from the bar length. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Delay and reverb calculator is a free, no-sign-up other tool. Fill in the 6 fields it asks for and it works out note length straight away, with the formula shown underneath. It suits whatever you happen to be working on. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Delay and reverb calculator work?
sections.html:
The Delay and reverb calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports note length in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the time signature, the preset and the pre-delay (Pre-delay and decay times)); then you type in the bar length.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in bpm.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 6 options, such as 2/2, 2/4 and 3/4. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 5 options, such as hall, large room and small room. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 15 options, such as 1/32nd, 1/32nd dotted and 1/32nd triplet. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 18 options, such as double whole, double whole dotted and double whole triplet. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

4 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Delay and reverb calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Note length=60000 × note length mod ÷ input your bpm...
Bar length mod=(1 ÷ 60000) × bar length × input your bpm...
Pre delay res 1=(input your bpm..., time signature, pre-delay, total delay ÷ reverb duration, 0, preset, pre-delay, total delay ÷ reverb duration)
Pre delay res 2=(input your bpm..., time signature, pre-delay, total delay ÷ reverb duration, 1, preset, pre-delay, total delay ÷ reverb duration)
Pre delay res 3=(input your bpm..., time signature, pre-delay, total delay ÷ reverb duration, 2, preset, pre-delay, total delay ÷ reverb duration)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Delay and reverb calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the bar length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Delay and reverb calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns note length, derived from the bar length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Delay and reverb calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the bar length, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Delay and reverb calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
